mcqs.question: A page loads noticeably faster on a repeat visit to the same domain than on the first visit, even though nothing about the HTML or assets is cached. What most likely changed?
options: DNS resolution hit a cache instead of doing a cold lookup through the resolver hierarchy
The server compressed the response body differently on the second visit
The browser skipped the TLS handshake entirely on the second visit
HTTP/2 multiplexing only becomes active starting from the second visit
mcqs.explanation: A cold DNS lookup can add 20-120ms; once the browser or OS resolver caches the answer, that cost disappears on the repeat visit even with nothing else cached. TLS still runs on a new connection, and HTTP/2 multiplexing is available from the first request, not gated by visit count.

mcqs.question: Why does TLS 1.3 typically add only one round trip to connection setup, versus TLS 1.2's two?
options: TLS 1.3 skips certificate validation for well-known certificate authorities
TLS 1.3 combines key exchange and cipher negotiation into the first flight of messages instead of a separate round trip
TLS 1.3 reuses the preceding TCP handshake, so it needs no additional round trip
TLS 1.3 only encrypts the response and not the request, halving negotiation work
mcqs.explanation: TLS 1.3's handshake redesign lets the client propose a key share immediately, collapsing what used to be two separate round trips into one. Certificate validation still happens, and TLS runs on top of the TCP connection, not as a substitute for part of it.

mcqs.question: A very large HTML document with a slow-to-finish tail still shows its header quickly in the browser. Why?
options: The browser silently truncates large documents past a fixed byte limit
The server always sends header markup over a separate, faster connection
The HTML parser tokenizes and builds the DOM incrementally as bytes stream in, rather than waiting for the full response
Browsers cache page headers from a previous, unrelated visit to any site
mcqs.explanation: The parser works against a stream, not a completed buffer, so content near the top of the document can be tokenized and rendered while later bytes are still in flight. There's no truncation or cross-visit header caching involved.

mcqs.question: In a cold HTTPS navigation, which pair of steps most commonly overlaps rather than running strictly one after the other?
options: DNS resolution and the TCP handshake
The TLS handshake and sending the HTTP request
HTML streaming/parsing and subresource fetches kicked off by the preload scanner
URL parsing and DNS resolution
mcqs.explanation: The preload scanner races ahead of the main parser to queue subresource requests, so those downloads proceed in parallel with ongoing HTML parsing. DNS, TCP, TLS and URL parsing are each prerequisites for the step that follows them and can't overlap that way.

mcqs.question: A site enables HSTS. What actually changes about how the browser handles a future navigation to it?
options: The browser rewrites http:// to https:// before attempting any connection, avoiding a redirect round trip
The browser skips DNS resolution entirely for that host going forward
The site's TLS certificate no longer needs to be validated on later visits
The browser automatically stores the entire page in bfcache after one HSTS-protected visit
mcqs.explanation: HSTS makes the browser itself upgrade the scheme locally before issuing any request, which is exactly what removes the extra redirect round trip a plain 301-based upgrade would have cost. It doesn't touch DNS caching, certificate validation, or bfcache eligibility.
